The company president was being extorted and had to deliver a ransom during a hostage exchange. The extortionists demanded a specific amount substantially greater than one million yen, and he could only raise about one million yen of the money to give them.

He knew the hostage would only be released if the payment appeared to satisfy the demand. A bag visibly containing just the one million yen would either be recognized as short or, worse, signal that he was holding back money—putting him and the hostage at risk. So he added more cash of his own, bringing the bag's total above one million yen but still short of the demanded amount.

The purpose of the added cash was deceptive bulk: it made the pile of money look plausible as the larger demanded sum, so that at the handover the extortionists would glance at the thick bundle, assume the demand had been met, and release the hostage without carefully counting. By the time they discovered the shortfall, the exchange would already be complete. He accepted losing all the cash, including the extra he had added, since the bag was to be handed over and kept—his goal was to get the hostage released, not to recover the money.

The man was being blackmailed and had to deliver a ransom, with a hostage to be exchanged. The extortionists had named a sum substantially larger than one million yen. He could raise only about one million yen of cash, then added cash of his own, so the bag held more than one million yen but still less than the full demand.

His central worry was for his own safety: he feared that if the extortionists discovered the bag contained exactly one million yen—the precise, recognizable sum that would reveal he had not properly met their much larger demand—they would turn on him. Simply handing over one million yen would therefore be dangerous.

By adding extra cash, he made the bag's total no longer exactly one million yen. The fuller pile of cash was meant to look consistent with the much larger sum they demanded, so that at the exchange the extortionists would believe they had received the full amount and would not scrutinize or count it closely. Even though the bag was actually still short, that mistaken belief was what he needed to get through the handover safely. The money, including the cash he had added, was handed over for good; he was trading a bit more money for his own protection.

The man was being extorted: an unavoidable situation forced him to deliver a ransom payment, with a hostage to be released in exchange. The extortionists named a sum substantially larger than one million yen, and he intended the one million yen to be part of that payment.

He feared for his own safety because of what the bag would be seen to contain. He worried that if the criminals discovered the bag held precisely one million yen—short of what they demanded—the deception would fail and they would turn on him. So he added more of his own cash to the bag, making its total exceed one million yen while it remained less than the full demanded amount.

The point of the added cash was to deceive the extortionists into believing they had received the entire amount they demanded. With the larger pile of cash, he hoped that at the handover they would look at the thick bundle, assume the demand had been satisfied, and not carefully count or scrutinize it; the shortfall would not be noticed until it was too late. That mistaken belief was what he wanted in order to protect himself and get through the exchange.

The money—including the extra cash he had contributed—was handed over and kept by the extortionists; he never expected to recover it. He was deliberately sacrificing a larger sum than the one million yen in order to create the appearance that the full demand had been met, thereby protecting himself from the extortionists.
